ev.title: The Real State of the American Consumer

kshape.lede: Higher-income households keep spending; lower-income households are under real strain, and the middle is starting to crack.
points: Fast food is losing lower-income customers at a high-single-digit rate year over year after raising prices about 40% since COVID against roughly 24% wage growth. Higher gas prices and fading tax-refund support are squeezing the same households.
Ralph Lauren raised average prices about 60% since 2018 and is still winning; steakhouses like Longhorn are running 10–11% same-store sales.
Credit card delinquencies and trading down are spreading up the income ladder. Walmart is now picking up $150K+ households through Walmart+.
Off-price is taking share across income groups: TJ Maxx +6% and Ross +17% same-store sales. Amazon, Walmart and Costco together take about 24% of U.S. retail sales.

news.h: Michigan sentiment rebounds to 51.0 in early November
news.w: The preliminary reading rose from 48.0 in October, beating the 48.0 forecast. Year-ahead inflation expectations eased to 4.3% from 4.7% and long-run to 3.4% from 3.5%.

news.h: Large Outback franchisee files for bankruptcy after closing 10 restaurants
news.w: Out West Restaurant Group, which runs 61 Outback Steakhouses in five western states, filed Chapter 11 after closing 10 restaurants in October; Bloomin' Brands agreed to buy its assets for $26.3 million.

news.h: Costco October comps +11.1%; +7.3% excluding gas and FX
news.w: Net sales rose 12.6% to $24.5B for the four weeks ended November 1. U.S. comps were 8.1% excluding gas and FX, and digital sales grew 22.5%.

news.h: More shoppers are delaying and canceling big purchases
news.w: In an October survey, 20% delayed and 11.1% canceled a major purchase in the past 90 days, mostly over high prices; 47.5% have three months of savings or less. Optimism about the economy ticked up to 30.2%.

news.h: Amazon Q3 sales up 12% to $201.9B; North America retail +6%
news.w: Online store sales grew only 2% (Prime Day moved into Q2). Q4 guidance of $240–247B implies a solid holiday quarter. Amazon is lifting U.S. warehouse starting pay to $20 an hour.

news.h: Saving rate falls to 3.8% as real spending stalls
news.w: September spending rose 0.5% but only matched inflation (real spending flat). Incomes grew 0.2%, so households saved less. PCE inflation is 3.6% over the year, core 3.1%.

news.h: NRF: consumers remain the bright spot heading into the holidays
news.w: Consumer spending drove almost 80% of GDP growth over the past four quarters. 64% of shoppers plan to wait for Thanksgiving weekend deals and 56% say the economy will affect their spending.
Up from 84.2 in September; the expectations index rose to 72.6 but remains below the 80 level that often signals recession risk.

news.h: Michigan sentiment ends October at 48.0, near record lows
news.w: Revised up from a preliminary 46.3. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7% and long-run to 3.5%; durable-goods buying conditions fell 18%.

news.h: NRF forecasts holiday sales to top $1 trillion, up 4.2%
news.w: Forecast of $1.013 trillion for November–December vs. 3.1% growth last year; 325,000–375,000 seasonal hires. NRF expects about half the growth to be real, the rest price increases.

news.h: September retail sales up 0.8%, but mostly at the pump
news.w: Excluding gas stations, sales rose just 0.2%. Department stores (+1.6%), furniture (+1.3%) and restaurants (+1.1%) gained; August was revised up to +1.3%.

news.h: Card spending up 6.2% a year in September
news.w: Per-household card spending growth (5.1% excluding gas) was among the strongest of the past four years, with lower- and middle-income households recovering.

v.notes: Wage growth is the Atlanta Fed’s 3-month moving average of median hourly wage growth from a year earlier, for the same workers (unweighted). "Lower half" and "upper half" split workers by where their wage sits in the distribution. Real wage growth here = wage growth minus CPI inflation for the same month. Real retail sales are Census retail and food services sales adjusted for CPI. Federal data for October 2025 were not collected during the government shutdown, so that month is blank. The Michigan reading for October 2026 is the final release; FRED adds it with a lag.
re: Walmart, Costco, TJ Maxx, Ross and other off-price and grocery tenants are taking share from every income group. Centers anchored by them carry the strongest tenant credit right now.
Lululemon, Nike and mall-based apparel are losing traffic; 2026 closures so far are led by apparel (about a third of the total). Check rollover exposure to these categories.
Value-priced and steakhouse concepts are growing; fast food that over-raised prices is losing lower-income guests. Restaurant pad credit depends on which side of that line a tenant sits.
The saving rate is at its lowest since 2022 and lower-income shoppers are stretched by gas prices. For multifamily and student housing, that argues for watching collections and concessions closely.

bofa.note: Spending growth spans all income groups, with lower- and middle-income households recovering. Buy-now-pay-later use is rising; nearly one in five BNPL households has a repayment above $500.

um.note: Current conditions hit an all-time low of 44.7 in the preliminary October reading, led by durable-goods buying conditions.

items.next: On the ballot today. If it passes, it takes effect about a month after the election and the state housing office writes the rules.
items.what: Would let single-family homes be built by right on lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of frontage and public water and sewer, in any district that allows homes. Towns keep control of setbacks, height, parking and short-term rentals. Boston is excluded because it has its own zoning law.
items.who: Legalize Starter Homes (chair Andrew Mikula); backed by Abundant Housing MA and the Greater Boston, Worcester and Plymouth chambers. Opposed by the Massachusetts Municipal Association. The Legislature's initiative-petition committee recommended no action.
items.why: Opens smaller-lot infill in sewered suburbs inside Route 128 and on the South Shore, which adds for-sale competition at the entry level but also creates small-lot development sites. Tufts projects 350 to 1,200 extra homes a year statewide; the campaign says 2,200 to 5,700.

items.b: Economic development bill (House amendment 71, Senate amendment 12); standalone S.998 / H.1544
items.next: In the six-member conference committee on the economic development bill. The session's last day to finish bills is Jan 5, 2027; no timeline has been announced.
items.what: Gives tenants in multifamily buildings the right to match a third-party offer and buy their building, or assign that right to a nonprofit, land trust or housing authority. Landlords must notify tenants before a sale. The House version is a statewide local option with small owners exempt; the Senate version is a five-year pilot in five communities.
items.who: Conferees: Reps. Aaron Michlewitz, Carole Fiola, Michael Soter; Sens. Barry Finegold, Michael Rodrigues, Peter Durant. Sen. Patricia Jehlen is a lead advocate.
items.why: Adds notice periods and a matching right to sales of Boston-area apartment buildings in any community that opts in, which can slow closings and narrow the buyer pool for value-add multifamily.

items.next: Only in the Senate bill, so the conference committee decides whether it survives. Deadline Jan 5, 2027.
items.what: Would allow two-family homes wherever single-family homes are allowed, as long as local dimensional rules are not overly restrictive. Towns could still set height and design standards.
items.who: Senate leadership; Sen. Julian Cyr spoke for it. Same six conferees as TOPA, led by Rep. Aaron Michlewitz and Sen. Barry Finegold.
items.why: Effectively ends single-family-only zoning, which would let owners add a unit to many suburban lots and raise land values for small infill sites.

items.b: Economic development bill (House H.5562 and Senate versions)
items.next: In both chambers' bills, so it is likely to be in the final version. Deadline Jan 5, 2027.
items.what: Defines site plan review as a compliance check against existing local standards, with objective rules, a 90-day decision deadline for by-right projects and automatic approval if a town misses it.
items.who: House passed its bill 148–2 in July; Senate passed its own version. Same six conferees as TOPA, led by Rep. Aaron Michlewitz and Sen. Barry Finegold.
items.why: Cuts one of the main ways towns slow by-right apartment and mixed-use projects, which shortens approval timelines and lowers carrying costs.

items.what: Both chambers create an opt-in program allowing residential conversion by right on commercially zoned lots, with parking limits near transit and state tax-credit preference for towns that join. The House bill alone lets religious institutions build multifamily housing by right on land they have owned at least three years (20% income-restricted, 45-foot height cap).
items.who: Same six conferees as TOPA, led by Rep. Aaron Michlewitz and Sen. Barry Finegold.
items.why: Directly relevant to repositioning older suburban office and retail sites into apartments in towns that opt in.

items.next: Talks slowed after the court removed the ballot question in June. Any bill would have to pass by Jan 5, 2027, or be refiled in the new session.
items.what: Would repeal the 1994 statewide ban on rent control and let cities and towns opt in to caps of inflation plus 5%, with a 10% ceiling. New construction and small owner-occupied buildings would be exempt.
items.who: Keep Massachusetts Home, working with developers HYM and WinnCompanies. Gov. Healey and Mayors Wu and Wilson called for a compromise. Housing for Massachusetts, the real estate-backed opponent, called parts of it problematic.
items.why: If revived, Boston, Somerville and Cambridge would be the likeliest adopters, which would cap rent growth on existing Greater Boston apartments.

items.next: Supporters would have to start a new petition; one law firm's analysis sees 2028 as the earliest likely ballot.
items.t: Statewide rent cap ballot question removed
items.what: Would have capped annual rent increases statewide at inflation or 5%, whichever is lower, in all 351 communities. The Supreme Judicial Court ruled unanimously that a religious exemption made it ineligible for the ballot.
items.why: Removes the near-term risk of a statewide cap; Boston's 2023 home-rule petition for rent stabilization still lacks legislative approval.

items.next: In effect since it was signed.
items.what: Replaces the "substantial hardship" test for variances with "practical difficulty," lets boards weigh the public interest in housing, explicitly allows use variances for housing, and extends how long a variance lasts from one to two years.
items.why: Makes it easier to get relief for odd lots and conversions without a full rezoning.

items.t: Sales-tax break on multifamily building materials
items.what: Exempts materials for multifamily construction from sales tax in census tracts with median income below 120% of area median, or where at least 15% of units are income-restricted.
items.why: Lowers hard costs on qualifying apartment projects at a time when construction input prices are up 11.7% from a year earlier.

items.t: Landlords pay the broker they hire
items.what: Since Aug 1, 2025, the party that hires a residential rental broker pays the fee, so tenants no longer pay a landlord's broker.
items.why: Shifts leasing costs onto owners who use brokers; budget it as an operating or turnover cost.

items.t: Apartments by right in commercial zones
items.what: Makes multifamily housing in commercial zones allowed by right. Towns may limit only frontage, setbacks and height (no stricter than for commercial buildings), cannot cap density, can require at most one parking space per unit and cannot require garages. Developers wrongly denied can seek attorney's fees.
items.who: Signed by Gov. Ayotte. House Housing chair Rep. Joe Alexander (R-Goffstown) backed it.
items.why: Opens commercially zoned land across the Seacoast and southern NH to apartments without density fights, a direct opportunity for mixed-use and multifamily development.

items.next: Signed; the signing date was not reported.
items.what: Lets towns require traffic, water and sewer studies before approving housing in commercial zones and deny projects the infrastructure cannot handle, but gives developers a "right to remedy" by paying for or building the needed upgrades.
items.why: Adds study costs and possible off-site improvement costs to NH commercial-zone projects, partly offsetting HB 1588.

items.next: Became law; the signing date was not reported.
items.t: No caps on dead-end road housing
items.what: Bars towns from capping road length or the number of homes on dead-end streets when the state fire code is met, and requires them to allow septic and electric lines in subdivision buffers and open space, except wetlands and protected shoreland.
items.who: Sponsor: Sen. Daniel Innis (R). Signed by Gov. Ayotte.
items.why: Makes more rural and suburban NH subdivision land buildable, especially for townhome and single-family projects.

items.t: Towns must allow multifamily in commercial zones
items.what: Bars cities and towns from prohibiting multifamily housing in commercial zones, subject to road, water, sewer and site conditions. HB 1588 and HB 1010 amended it this year.
items.why: The base law that opened commercial land in NH to apartments.

items.t: Landlords can decline to renew at lease end
items.what: Lets landlords end a tenancy when a lease expires without stating a cause, with at least 60 days' notice that the lease won't be renewed. Before this, most NH tenants could only be evicted for specific causes.
items.who: Sponsor: Rep. Bob Lynn (R-Windham). Signed by Gov. Ayotte in 2025.
items.why: Gives NH owners more flexibility to reposition or renovate units at lease expiration.

v.h: October payrolls jump 165,000, far above forecasts; unemployment falls to 4.1%
v.s: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October versus forecasts of roughly 59,000–65,000, and August and September were revised up a combined 84,000 (September to 60,000 from 29,000). Unemployment slipped to 4.1% from 4.2%, and average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year. Professional and business services added 70,000 and health care 42,000; construction changed little. The 2-year rose 5 bp to 4.51% and the 10-year 2 bp to 4.86%.
v.w: A firm job market makes a December hike more likely, which would raise SOFR-based floating and bridge loan costs, though fixed-rate quotes tied to the 10-year barely moved.

v.h: December hike odds climb to 77% from 69%
v.s: After the jobs report, Kalshi priced a Dec 9 hike at 77.5% and Polymarket at 76.5% (Nov 6, 11:30 AM ET), up from about 69% on Thursday. Kalshi's meeting table put a January 2027 hike at 21% and March at 42%, down from 24% and 55% a day earlier.
v.w: Markets now see a December hike as likely but fewer follow-up hikes, which keeps short-term floating rates rising while capping how far long rates climb.

v.h: Question 7 defeated: voters reject smaller-lot starter homes, AP says
v.s: The AP called the starter-homes question early Friday afternoon; with 98.99% counted, "no" led by 32,322 votes out of about 2.54 million, roughly 1.2 points (unofficial). It would have barred minimum lot sizes above 5,000 SF for parcels with water, sewer and 50 feet of frontage; a Tufts researcher estimated 350 to 1,200 homes a year. Lawmakers are still negotiating an economic development bill that includes statewide duplexes and multifamily housing on religious land.
v.w: Suburban zoning stays local, so new for-sale supply around Boston remains scarce, which supports existing single-family and condo values and pushes the zoning fight back to the Legislature.

v.h: Stocks recover part of Thursday's rout; S&P 500 ends the week down 2.7%
v.s: The Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579 and the S&P 500 0.32% to 7,376 as chip stocks bounced, while the Dow fell 0.46% to 51,286. For the week the S&P 500 lost 2.68%, the Nasdaq 3.37% and the Dow 0.94%. Brent settled at $98.32, down sharply for the week, and the VIX eased to 25.64 from 28.18.
v.w: Volatility is easing but remains high, which tends to keep credit spreads wide and makes lenders more cautious on lab and tech-tenant exposure.

v.h: Westborough shopping center anchored by Stop & Shop and Staples heads to foreclosure auction
v.s: First Tech Federal Credit Union scheduled a Dec 8 auction of 18 and 30 Lyman St. on Route 9, five buildings totaling 371,425 SF owned by Colangelo Massachusetts Real Estate LLC, which took a $30.75M mortgage in December 2022. The town assesses the two parcels at $12.9M and $15.8M.
v.w: A grocery-anchored center going to auction suggests suburban retail debt maturities are straining even well-tenanted assets, and the result will set a pricing marker for MetroWest retail.

v.h: Revere weighs a 40R district for a 39-acre public housing redevelopment
v.s: The Revere Housing Authority wants to rebuild its 1950s Cooledge Street site, raising public housing to 790 units from 431 and adding 910 market-rate units, 1,700 in all. The City Council began reviewing a Chapter 40R overlay in late October; construction could start in four to five years.
v.w: A large mixed-income pipeline north of Boston would add rental supply on a long timeline, after 2030.

v.h: Developer seeks to triple a Brighton apartment project to 143 units
v.s: DND Homes filed to expand Dighton Gardens at 25–37 Dighton St. from an approved 44-unit, four-story building to a six-story, 93,612 SF building with 143 apartments and 30 parking spaces; MountainOne Bank provided $4.7M of site financing in March.
v.w: Developers are seeking more density to make Boston rental projects pencil at today's construction and financing costs.

v.h: AI stock rout sinks the Nasdaq 5.5% into a correction; 2-year yield falls 12 bp to 4.46%
v.s: The Nasdaq fell 5.52% to 24,315, closing in correction territory, the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Dow 1,833 points (3.44%) to 51,523, erasing Wednesday's post-election rally; the Philadelphia chip index fell 12.3% and the VIX jumped 11.57 points to 28.18. Investors sold this year's AI winners, and analysts tied part of the drop to Democrats' wins and possible limits on data-center growth. Money moved into Treasuries: the 2-year fell 12 bp to 4.46%, its biggest drop since Oct 22, the 5-year 10 bp to 4.59%, the 10-year 6 bp to 4.84% and the 30-year 3 bp to 5.25% (U.S. Treasury). Brent settled at $98.29, up about 3.9%.
v.src: Yahoo Finance / Fox Business / U.S. Treasury
v.w: The 10-year is now 47 bp below its Oct 5 high, which lowers fixed-rate loan quotes, but a sharp risk-off move tends to widen credit spreads and could slow lab and data-center leasing tied to tech tenants.

v.h: December hike odds fall to 69% from 80%
v.s: Kalshi priced a Dec 9 hike at 69% and Polymarket at 69.5% on Thursday at 11:28 AM ET, during the stock selloff, down from about 80% on Wednesday. Kalshi's January 2027 hike odds slipped to about 24% from 26%; March is about 55%. The Bank of England raised its rate a quarter point to 4%, its first hike since 2023.
v.w: A December hike is still favored, so SOFR-based floating and bridge loans likely cost about 25 bp more next year, but the odds are moving with stocks and Friday's jobs report.

v.h: Freddie Mac 30-year rate falls to 7.18%, a third straight weekly decline
v.s: The 30-year fixed averaged 7.18%, down from 7.24%, and the 15-year 6.57%, down from 6.60%; a year ago the 30-year was 6.22%. Mortgage News Daily's daily index fell 5 bp to 7.17% on Thursday.
v.w: Lower rates help condo and small multifamily exits at the margin, but buyers still pay about a point more than a year ago, which keeps many would-be buyers renting.

v.h: Question 7 trails 50.6% to 49.4% with 98% counted; AP has not called it
v.s: The starter-homes question, which would allow single-family homes on 5,000 SF lots with water and sewer outside Boston, was behind by about 1.2 points with 98% of ballots counted Thursday afternoon (AP). The Boston Business Journal said it appears on track to narrowly fail; backers are looking to remaining mail-in ballots.
v.src: Greenfield Recorder (AP) / Boston Business Journal via NBC Boston
v.w: If it fails, suburban lot-size rules stay with each town, keeping small-lot infill and new for-sale supply limited around Boston.

v.h: Jobless claims fall to 189,000; announced layoffs lowest since 2023
v.s: Initial jobless claims fell 6,000 to 189,000 in the week ended Oct 31, below the 197,000 forecast. Challenger counted 43,994 announced job cuts in October, down 71% from a year earlier and the fewest since 2023. Economists expect about 59,000 jobs in Friday's October report (Dow Jones) after September's 29,000.
v.w: Few layoffs support rent collections and office and retail occupancy even as hiring stays slow.

v.h: Healthpeak to buy a West Cambridge building for $36M
v.s: Healthpeak said on its third-quarter call that it agreed to buy a building at Cambridge Discovery Park off Route 2, occupied by the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, for $36M; the deal is pending. Healthpeak bought a controlling interest in the four-building, 605,000 SF campus for $664M in 2020, and CBRE was recently named leasing agent.
v.w: A REIT adding to its Alewife holdings while other Cambridge lab and office trades are pricing well below past values.

v.h: Malden cuts affordable-housing requirement to 10% from 15%
v.s: Malden's council voted to lower the share of income-restricted units in projects of eight or more units to 10% from 15%, raise the rental income limit to 60% of area median income from 50%, and give two bonus units for each affordable unit. A second vote is set for Nov 10. Waltham and Chelsea also rolled back requirements this year, and Cambridge is reviewing its rules.
v.w: Looser inclusionary rules improve project math for new apartments in Malden and nearby cities where construction has slowed.

v.h: Massachusetts active home listings up 24.9% from a year earlier in October
v.s: Realtor.com counted 24.9% more active listings in Massachusetts in October than a year earlier and 4.6% more new listings. Nationally, active listings rose 7.4% to 1.18 million while new listings fell 7.5%, the steepest drop of 2026.
v.w: More for-sale inventory gives buyers leverage on condos and small multifamily, which can weigh on exit pricing.

v.h: Democrats win Congress; Dow jumps 1,569 points, Brent falls 8.6% and the 10-year closes at 4.90%
v.s: The AP called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday. The Dow rose 1,569 points (3.0%) to 53,356, its best day since April 2025, the S&P 500 gained 1.6% to about 7,689 and the Nasdaq 1.4%, while the VIX fell 4.2 points to 16.6. Brent fell 8.6% to $94.64, down about 17% since Oct 30, on hopes of pressure to pull back from the U.S.–Iran war; Iran's Revolutionary Guard said four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The 10-year closed at 4.90%, down 5 bp, the 2-year at 4.58% and the 30-year at 5.28% (U.S. Treasury). Energy and defense stocks fell; HCA rose 10.3%.
v.src: AP via Boston.com / TheStreet / U.S. Treasury
v.w: Lower oil and long yields ease fuel, heating and fixed-rate borrowing costs, but the oil drop rests on hopes for less U.S. military engagement in Iran and could reverse; a Democratic Congress from January adds uncertainty to the administration's agenda.

v.h: IWG adds six flexible office locations in Massachusetts
v.s: International Workplace Group opened or signed six new Regus and HQ locations in Boston, Worcester, Somerville, North Andover, Holbrook and Charlestown, bringing its Massachusetts total to 50; five are open and Charlestown opens in the first quarter. Separately, the owner of the 140-acre Stone-E-Lea golf course in Attleboro is preparing to sell it for redevelopment through 128 CRE.
v.w: Flex operators taking suburban and South Shore space is a small source of office demand at a time when single-tenant suburban buildings are selling at deep discounts.

v.h: December hike odds jump to about 80% from 72%
v.s: Kalshi priced a Dec 9 hike at 80.5% and Polymarket at 79.5% on Wednesday at 11:21 AM ET, up from about 72% in a Nov 3 snapshot taken before Tuesday's job openings report. Kalshi's January 2027 hike odds fell to about 26% from 31% a week earlier; March is about 51%.
v.w: A December hike to 4.00–4.25% now looks more likely, which would add about 25 bp to SOFR-based floating-rate and bridge loans even as long-term fixed rates ease.

v.h: Treasury holds refunding sizes at $125B but softens its guidance
v.s: Treasury will sell $58B of 3-year notes on Nov 9, $42B of 10-year notes on Nov 10 and $25B of 30-year bonds on Nov 12, refunding about $97B of maturing debt and raising about $28B of new cash. It now says it anticipates maintaining coupon and FRN sizes "for the next several quarters," dropping "at least"; analysts read that as room for changes in the first half of 2027. It plans up to $70B of liquidity buybacks next quarter and will review buyback limits.
v.src: U.S. Treasury via Seeking Alpha / Bloomberg via AOL
v.w: Steady sizes ease near-term supply worries, but the softer wording and $800B of Jan–Mar borrowing keep a floor under the long-term yields that price fixed-rate CRE loans.

v.h: Starter-homes Question 7 too close to call; Healey and Ayotte reelected
v.s: Question 7, which would allow single-family homes on 5,000 SF lots with public water and sewer outside Boston, led 50.8% to 49.2% with about 49% of votes counted at 12:30 AM Wednesday. Gov. Maura Healey won reelection in Massachusetts and Gov. Kelly Ayotte a second term in New Hampshire (AP); Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire's open Senate seat over John Sununu.
v.w: If Question 7 passes, small-lot infill opens in sewered suburbs; both governors' housing and zoning agendas carry into 2027.

v.h: BioMed sells 210 Broadway near Kendall Square for $15.1M, 36% below its 2012 price
v.s: Bulfinch Companies bought the 64,812 SF building, completed in 1999, for about $233/SF; BioMed paid $23.5M in 2012 and Cambridge assesses it at $27M. LoopNet lists two available spaces of 3,181 to 18,781 SF.
v.w: Another Cambridge office trade well below its prior price and assessed value, a fresh comp for older space on the edge of Kendall Square.

v.h: Mattapan garage sells for $8.75M for a 105-unit affordable project
v.s: The Planning Office for Urban Affairs and JGE Development are behind the purchase of 1590 Blue Hill Ave., a 1.6-acre auto site, from the McKeen family. The BPDA approved a six-story, 105-unit income-restricted building in August, estimated at $72.3M; securing construction financing is expected to take at least two years.
v.w: Land for affordable housing along Blue Hill Ave. traded at about $83K per approved unit, with a long financing runway before any new supply.

v.h: 10-year rises 4 bp to 4.95% as job openings beat forecasts
v.s: The 10-year closed at 4.95% on Tuesday (U.S. Treasury), up from 4.91% on Monday and 1 bp above last Friday's 4.94%; the 2-year rose to 4.61% and the 30-year to 5.32%. September job openings came in at 7.52M against 7.10M expected, and Treasury trimmed its fourth-quarter borrowing estimate. Traders also positioned for the midterm elections (Trading Economics).
v.w: October's 35 bp rally in the 10-year is holding, but a firm labor market keeps a December hike in play; fixed-rate borrowers still have lower rates than a month ago, while SOFR loans face a likely increase.

v.h: Job openings jump to 7.52M in September, the most since May
v.s: Openings rose from a revised 7.19M in August against forecasts of about 7.10M. Quits rose to 3.37M, the most in about 18 months, and layoffs fell to 1.64M, the lowest since March 2025. Forecasters expect about 65,000 jobs in Friday's October report after September's 29,000.
v.src: BLS / AP via WSLS / 24/7 Wall St.
v.w: Strong labor demand supports rent growth and tenant demand, but it also argues for the Fed to keep hiking, which keeps floating-rate debt costly.

v.h: Former Lombardo's site in Randolph planned for 200-room hotel and dinner theater
v.s: Core Investments and A Yankee Line filed with MEPA for a 171K SF, 200-room hotel and a 65K SF events building with a 400-seat dinner theater on 13 acres off Scanlon Drive, linked by a pedestrian bridge, with 540 parking spaces and a trail to the Blue Hills. Core bought the site in 2022.
v.w: A sizable South Shore hospitality project on Route 128; it needs MEPA and state approvals and would test hotel financing at current rates.

v.h: Brent plunges about 8% to below $105 on a draft U.S.–Iran peace proposal
v.s: Brent fell 7.6% to $104.77 on Monday and WTI dropped below $100 after a draft proposal to end the U.S.–Iran war circulated following weekend talks in Qatar; Iran outlined a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if its demands, including an end to the U.S. naval blockade, are met. ING cautioned that new strikes could follow the midterm elections.
v.w: Lower oil would ease diesel, heating and construction-input costs and take pressure off inflation and yields, but the drop is headline-driven and could reverse quickly.

v.h: Treasury trims Oct–Dec borrowing estimate to $618B; sees $800B in Jan–Mar
v.s: Treasury expects to borrow $618B from private investors in October–December, $10B below its August estimate, mostly because it started the quarter with more cash; excluding that, the estimate is $24B higher. It expects $800B in January–March 2027, assuming a $1.0T end-of-March cash balance.
v.w: Heavy borrowing into early 2027 keeps a floor under long-term yields that set fixed-rate CRE loans.

v.h: ISM manufacturing rises to 55.5; prices paid ease to 75.2
v.s: The October index rose from 54.5 against 54.6 expected, the 10th straight month of expansion; production hit 59.0, the highest since November 2021. Prices paid eased to 75.2 from 77.9 but stayed high. Stocks extended their tech selloff: the Nasdaq fell 1.1% and the S&P 500 0.5% while the Dow rose 0.4%.
v.w: Strong factory activity supports industrial demand, while still-high input prices keep construction costs elevated.

v.h: High-yield spread jumps 18 bp to 344 bp on Oct 30; IG widens to 94 bp
v.s: The ICE BofA high-yield spread widened to 344 bp on Oct 30 as tech stocks fell, then eased to 343 bp on Nov 2 and 340 bp on Nov 3; it was 314 bp on Oct 28. The investment-grade spread rose to 94 bp from 89 bp and was 93 bp on Nov 3. The HY yield was 8.14% on Nov 3.
v.w: Wider credit spreads offset part of the Treasury rally for riskier borrowers and tend to show up in CMBS and bridge-loan pricing.

v.h: Gas and diesel ease as oil falls; AAA gasoline at $4.17
v.s: AAA's national average was $4.17 for gasoline, down 12¢ from a week earlier, and $6.29 for diesel, down 6¢. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90, and GasBuddy warned that volatility could return after the midterms.
v.w: Cheaper fuel helps tenants' budgets and building operating costs, but diesel is still about $2.60 above a year ago.

v.h: Worcester finishes the state's largest office-to-residential conversion
v.s: Synergy's Altitude Worcester turned the former Fallon Health tower at 24 Elm St. into 198 apartments, and a co-venture with POUA turned Two Chestnut Place into 22 affordable condos, for 220 homes in all.
v.w: A completed proof point for conversions as Boston's 75% tax abatement deadline (Dec 31) approaches.

v.h: Ion Bank completes purchase of Boston's The Cooperative Bank
v.s: Connecticut-based Ion Bank finished its acquisition of The Cooperative Bank, which will operate as a division.
v.w: Consolidation among local community banks can change who lends on small Boston-area CRE deals.

v.h: Central Mass. town's first apartments in decades draw 900+ applications for 54 units
v.s: A new multifamily project in a central Massachusetts town drew more than 900 applications for 54 apartments.
v.w: Shows deep unmet rental demand outside Route 128, where supply is thin.

v.h: Tech earnings rout sinks the Nasdaq about 3%; Intel falls 30%
v.s: The Nasdaq was down about 3.1% and the S&P 500 2.1% Friday afternoon. Intel fell about 30% after a weak fourth-quarter forecast that cited a PC slump and a factory accident in Israel, pulling AMD down 12% and Nvidia 5%; Amazon's results disappointed, and Reddit fell about 28% on a softer outlook. The Russell 2000 opened higher, and Regeneron, Veralto and CoStar rose on earnings beats.
v.w: A second straight day of big-tech losses is the main reason long rates fell that week; if AI spending doubts keep spreading, they help borrowers through lower Treasury yields even as they hurt REIT and lab tenants tied to tech.

v.h: 10-year falls toward 4.9%, capping its biggest monthly rally since 2024
v.s: The 10-year was about 4.93% Friday afternoon (Trading Economics), roughly 5 bp below Thursday's 4.98% close, after touching about 4.89%, the lowest since Sept 10. It is down about 36–40 bp in October from 5.29% on Sept 30, the biggest monthly drop since 2024, while the 2-year fell about 32 bp. Investors moved from tech stocks into Treasuries after Alphabet, Amazon and Intel results raised doubts about debt-funded AI spending.
v.w: The 10-year is now about 38 bp below its Oct 5 high of 5.31%; for a lender quoting off the 10-year, that is roughly a third of a point off fixed-rate debt since early October.

v.h: December hike odds slip to about 72% from 79%
v.s: Kalshi priced a 71.5% chance of a Dec 9 hike and Polymarket 72.5% on Friday at 11:26 AM ET, down from 79% on Kalshi on Thursday; CME FedWatch was also near 72% (Trading Economics). Kalshi put a January 2027 hike at about 26%, down from 33%. The move followed an in-line ECI report and the tech selloff.
v.w: A hike was still favored, so floating-rate and SOFR-based loans likely get more expensive in December.

v.h: Employment costs rise 0.8% in Q3; private wage growth slowest since 2021
v.s: The Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, as expected. Private-industry wages and salaries rose 3.1% from a year earlier, the slowest since early 2021, and total compensation 3.4%; benefits rose 3.9%, with employer health insurance costs up 6.4%. Real wages fell 0.6% over the year.
v.w: Cooling wage growth argues against a wage-driven inflation spiral, but falling real pay squeezes renters and retail spending.

v.h: Microsoft's $25B bond sale draws $115B of orders
v.s: Microsoft priced $25B of bonds in 10 tranches from 2 to 40 years on Oct 29, its first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017. Orders reached $115B, 4.6 times the deal, and the 40-year priced 105 bp over Treasuries, up to 30 bp inside initial guidance; Alphabet's 40-year trades about 28 bp wider.
v.w: Strong demand for top-rated corporate debt shows investors still have cash for long bonds, but heavy AI borrowing competes with real estate for the same buyers.

v.h: Brent climbs back toward $112.50 after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz
v.s: Brent was near $112.50 on Friday, up about 1.5% from Thursday, after tanker attacks and mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia; WTI was near $104.
v.w: Oil near $110+ kept diesel and heating costs high heading into winter, a direct hit to owner-paid utilities and construction budgets.

v.h: Stalled Newton development site sells at foreclosure auction for $6.5M
v.s: Trillennium Services, a Newton demolition contractor, won 283 Melrose St. in Auburndale with a $6.5M bid, topping lender Dedham Institution for Savings' $6.4M opening bid on a $9.4M 2018 loan. Townhouse construction was halted in 2023 for unpermitted work; the site carries about $16M of liens and fines and sits in Newton's Village Center Overlay District.
v.w: Another lender loss on a suburban residential site; the overlay zoning may let a new owner build more density than the stalled plan.

v.h: Boston's Hyatt Centric Faneuil Hall trades for $58.4M
v.s: EOS Investors of New York bought the 163-room hotel at 50–68 Devonshire St. from Magna Hospitality for $58.4M, about $358K per room, with $40M of Beacon Bank & Trust financing. Magna paid $16.5M in 2016 when Related sold the hotel portion of Congress Square.
v.w: Downtown hotels are still drawing outside capital and bank debt at a time when office in the same area sells at deep discounts.

v.h: 'Distress is finally trading': investors chase Boston office discounts
v.s: Boston office sales reached $2.2B in Q3, up 23.7% from a year earlier (Avison Young). Recent trades include 18 Tremont St. for $30M (Jamestown paid $103M in 2019), 10–20 Channel Center St. for $52M ($119M in 2016) and 100 Summer St. for $260M ($806M in 2019). Trepp counts $78B of CMBS loans reaching hard maturity from October 2026 through 2027.
v.w: Price discovery is happening deal by deal; these comps reset values for downtown office and the loans behind them.

v.h: December hike odds rise to about 79% after the Fed's split vote
v.s: Kalshi priced a 79% chance of a Dec 9 hike on Thursday morning (11:27 AM ET), up from 72.5% on Oct 26 evening, and Polymarket was 76.5%; futures were near 85% after Wednesday's decision (Bloomberg data). Kalshi put a January 2027 hike at about 33% and March at about 54%.
v.w: A December hike to 4.00–4.25% would lift SOFR-based floating-rate loan costs by another 25 bp heading into 2027.

v.h: 10-year falls 7 bp to 4.98% as PCE comes in line and GDP beats
v.s: The 10-year closed at 4.98% on Thursday by Treasury's measure, down 7 bp from Wednesday's 5.05%; the 2-year fell 6 bp to 4.61% and the 30-year 5 bp to 5.32%. September PCE prices rose 3.6% from a year earlier and core 3.1%, both in line with forecasts, while Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate vs. 3.2% expected. Treasury sold $44B of 7-year notes at 4.894%, right on the when-issued level, with a 2.46x bid-to-cover.
v.w: The 10-year moved back under 5%, a modest relief for fixed-rate loan quotes.

v.h: Alphabet drops 12% and the Nasdaq falls 1.4%; Microsoft launches a $25B+ bond sale
v.s: The Nasdaq fell 1.38% to 26,184.72 and the S&P 500 0.31% to 7,720.10 after Alphabet sank more than 12% on a search revenue miss, while the Russell 2000 rose 1.0% and 8 of 11 S&P sectors gained. Microsoft beat forecasts and launched at least $25B of bonds in 10 tranches from 2 to 40 years, its first U.S. bond sale since 2017. Amazon reported after the close: EPS of $1.89 vs. $1.97 expected.
v.w: AI spenders are borrowing heavily in the bond market, adding corporate supply that competes with real estate debt for the same investors.

v.h: Freddie Mac 30-year rate falls to 7.24%, the lowest this month
v.s: The 30-year fixed averaged 7.24% this week, down from 7.32% and the second straight weekly decline; the 15-year fell to 6.60% from 6.68%. A year ago the 30-year was 6.17%. Mortgage News Daily's daily index was 7.35% on Oct 28.
v.w: Lower rates help condo and small multifamily buyers at the margin, but rates still 107 bp above a year ago keep would-be buyers renting longer.

v.h: Greater Boston pending home sales fall 10.6% in September
v.s: Agents reported 3,374 newly pending sales of all home types in September, 10.6% fewer than a year earlier, as the average 30-year mortgage rate ended the month at 7.28%, up from 6.65% at the end of August.
v.w: Slower for-sale activity keeps households in the rental pool, which supports apartment occupancy around Boston.

v.h: Fed holds at 3.75–4.00%, but two officials vote for a hike
v.s: The Fed left its target range at 3.75–4.00% in a 10–2 vote; Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike. The statement upgraded growth to "strong" from "solid" and dropped language tying policy to a return to 2% inflation. Chair Warsh called the hikes so far "monetary medicine starting to work some" but said there were "no firm conclusions." The 10-year rose 6 bp to 5.05% on the day.
v.w: Two hike dissents show the committee leaning toward more tightening, so Boston and NH borrowers should expect no relief on short-term rates this year.

v.h: High-yield spread narrows 24 bp in three sessions to 314 bp
v.s: The ICE BofA high-yield spread fell to 314 bp on Oct 28 from 338 bp on Oct 23 and 340 bp on Oct 22; the investment-grade spread narrowed to 86 bp from 91 bp. The high-yield yield was 7.96% on Oct 27, down from 8.14% on Oct 23.
v.w: Tighter spreads lower all-in borrowing costs even with Treasuries flat, and improve the backdrop for CMBS and CRE CLO issuance.

v.h: South Weymouth air base plan readies a first phase of up to 2,700 homes
v.s: New England Development and Brookfield Properties, master developers since 2020, plan up to 2,700 units across 13 parcels in the first phase of the 1,400-acre site, with two apartment complexes set to start in March 2027. A $120M, 6.7-mile MWRA water pipeline is due by 2032; MassDevelopment and MassWorks have committed $35M over two years for water, sewer and roads.
v.w: A large new South Shore rental pipeline would add competition for Weymouth and Braintree apartments later this decade.

v.h: Apartment List: national rent dips 0.3% in October; Boston metro up 1.0% from a year ago
v.s: The national median was $1,384, down 0.3% on the month and up 0.1% from a year earlier; the vacancy index eased to 7.0% from a 7.3% peak in February, and 32% of multifamily properties offered at least a month free. The Boston metro median was $2,233, up 1.0%; Boston city fell 1.6% in October to $2,453.
v.w: Seasonal softening and widespread concessions argue for conservative near-term rent growth in underwriting, even in supply-constrained Boston.

v.h: Rockpoint buys back 100 Summer St. for $260M at foreclosure, 68% below its 2019 price
v.s: Rockpoint Group, the existing owner, was the only bidder at Tuesday's foreclosure auction of the 32-story, roughly 1.1M SF tower near South Station, paying the $260M opening bid, about $236/SF. Rockpoint paid $806M in 2019 with $470M of Wells Fargo financing. The building is 72% occupied; tenants include SimpliSafe and the Massachusetts Trial Court.
v.w: A third high-profile distressed downtown sale since early 2025 resets the price benchmark for older Class A towers to about a quarter of replacement-era values.

v.h: Alexandria to sell its unfinished 421 Park Drive lab tower in the Fenway
v.s: Alexandria Real Estate Equities agreed to sell the 13-story, 339,668 SF building to an unnamed institutional investor, with closing expected in Q4 2026; no price was disclosed. The buyer is expected to take on about $136M of remaining interior lab work. About 268,000 SF was sold to Boston Children's Hospital in 2023 as a condominium.
v.w: Even the largest lab owner is shedding development risk, a sign that Boston life science values have not found a floor.

v.h: Case-Shiller: home prices up 2.1% in August; Boston up 2.6%
v.s: The national index rose 2.1% from a year earlier in August (1.9% in July) and the 20-city composite 2.7%. Boston rose 2.6% over the year but fell 0.35% on the month. Chicago (+6.7%) led; Seattle (−2.0%) was weakest. Real home prices fell for a 15th straight month.
v.w: Flat real home prices and 7%+ mortgages keep ownership costly relative to renting in Greater Boston.

v.h: 5-year auction: $70B at 4.845% with firmer demand than September
v.s: Treasury sold $70B of 5-year notes at 4.845% with a 0.4 bp tail (0.9 bp average). The bid-to-cover was 2.33x vs. 2.21x in September; dealers took 10.6% vs. a 13.0% average. On Wednesday the $28B 2-year FRN drew a 3.05x bid-to-cover at a 0.038% high margin.
v.w: Steady demand at the belly of the curve, where most 5-year CRE loans are priced, eases fears of a buyers' strike.

v.h: Diesel rises 7.6¢ to $6.352; New England gasoline dips to $4.199
v.s: EIA's Oct 26 survey showed U.S. diesel up 7.6¢ to $6.352, $2.634 above a year ago, and regular gasoline down 1.5¢ to $4.269. In New England, diesel fell 4.9¢ to $6.421 and gasoline 5.0¢ to $4.199; Boston gasoline was $4.176.
v.w: Diesel near $6.40 in New England keeps construction, trucking and heating oil costs high for owners into winter.

v.h: Zumper: Boston 1-bedroom rent slips 0.7% in October to $2,980
v.s: Boston ranked third nationally for 1-bedroom rent at $2,980, up 2.8% from a year earlier but down 0.7% on the month; 2-bedrooms were $3,500, up 1.4%. Nationally the 1-bedroom median was $1,519 (+0.5% YoY) and the 2-bedroom $1,901 (+0.7%). Providence 1-bedrooms rose 8.8% and New Haven 5.6%.
v.w: Boston rents are still rising faster than the national average but cooling into winter, which matters for renewal assumptions on Greater Boston multifamily.

v.h: 10-year holds at 5.00% as the $69B 2-year auction tails
v.s: The 10-year closed at 5.00% on Monday by Treasury's measure, unchanged from Friday and 15 bp below its 5.15% close a week earlier, after the Oct 22 flight-to-safety drop. The 2-year was 4.68% and the 30-year 5.31%. Treasury sold $69B of 2-year notes at 4.708%, a 0.3 bp tail, with a 2.59x bid-to-cover vs. a 2.64x average; dealers took 13.0% vs. an 11.3% average.
v.w: Yields held most of the prior week's drop, but a soft start to $211B of note sales showed demand was still price-sensitive heading into the Fed decision.

v.h: Brent slips to $115.81 as mediators meet Iranian officials in Tehran
v.s: Brent settled at $115.81, down 91 cents, and WTI at $101.76, down $1.51, on hopes that talks in Tehran involving Qatari mediators and Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials could ease hostilities. Houthi attacks on Saudi pumping stations and reports that U.S. forces could strike Iran within 96 hours of an order limited the decline.
v.w: Oil near $116 fed diesel, heating oil and construction costs; a diplomatic breakthrough would be the clearest path to lower inflation and yields.

v.h: Anthropic files public S-1 for Nasdaq IPO; Nasdaq rises 0.8%
v.s: Anthropic made its S-1 public on Monday to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with 22 banks led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley; the price range is still blank. The filing shows first-half revenue of $16.3B and a mostly non-cash $80.7B net loss. The Wall Street Journal reported a listing targeted for the week of Nov 16, and people familiar with the matter said it could raise $100B or more. Separately, Meta said it plans to raise up to $95B in stock for AI data centers.
v.w: A record-size equity raise, plus Meta's stock sale, shows AI spending shifting toward equity funding, which could ease some of the pressure on credit markets that has kept CRE loan spreads wide.

v.h: Eastern Bank reports record income growth in Q3
v.s: Eastern Bank said overall income rose 50% in the third quarter and net interest income rose by more than $57M.
v.w: Strong earnings at a large local lender support its capacity to make commercial real estate loans in Greater Boston.

v.h: Flash PMI: selling prices rise at the fastest pace in more than four years
v.s: S&P Global's flash October manufacturing PMI rose to 56.0 from 55.9, above the 55.5 expected, while services fell to 57.9 from 58.8 and the composite to 57.6 from 58.4. The survey showed the sharpest increase in selling prices in more than four years as oil costs spread through goods and services.
v.w: Firm activity and faster price increases argue against a growth scare and keep a December hike on the table.

v.h: Vigilant Holdings buys Londonderry industrial building for $16.6M
v.s: Vigilant Holdings bought 13 Page Rd. in Londonderry, a fully leased 75,480 SF Class A industrial building completed in 2025, from an affiliate of Rhino Capital Advisors for $16.6M, about $220/SF. Bar Harbor Bank & Trust provided an $11.45M five-year fixed-rate acquisition loan; JLL represented the seller.
v.w: JLL says the pricing gap between southern New Hampshire and gateway markets is narrowing, and local banks are still lending on new, leased industrial.

v.h: 24-unit Brighton apartment building sells for $8.875M
v.s: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 15 Euston Rd., a 24-unit building in Brighton, for $8.875M, about $370,000 per unit, after a record number of groups toured the property.
v.w: Deep buyer interest in small Boston multifamily contrasts with distress elsewhere in Brighton, such as the Selkirk Place foreclosure auction set for Oct 28.

v.h: Brent settles at $116.72 as fears of renewed U.S. strikes on Iran grow
v.s: Brent crude for December rose about 3.4% to settle at $116.72, its third straight weekly gain, and WTI traded near $104. Reports said U.S. and Israeli officials drew up plans for renewed strikes on Iran, the State Department ordered non-essential staff to leave, and Saudi Aramco reportedly told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters.
v.w: Higher oil fed diesel, heating oil and construction costs and kept inflation high.

v.h: FoxRock buys Quincy office building for $5.5M, 78% below its 2013 price
v.s: FoxRock Properties bought 1100 Crown Colony Drive in Quincy, a 132,000 SF office building, from W.P. Carey for $5.5M, per an Oct. 21 deed, about $42/SF. W.P. Carey paid $25.5M in 2013. Sole tenant Arbella Insurance is moving next door to 1200 Crown Colony, which FoxRock also owns.
v.w: A South Shore suburban office comp at about $42/SF shows how far single-tenant office values fall once the tenant leaves.

v.h: 10-year ends the week at 5.00%, 9 bp below the prior Friday
v.s: The 10-year closed at 5.00% on Friday by Treasury's measure, up 4 bp from Thursday's 4.96% close but 9 bp below the prior Friday's 5.09%. Stocks slipped: the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Dow 1.2%, while the Nasdaq dipped 0.2% after Thursday's 2.6% drop.
v.w: Treasuries held most of Thursday's rally despite higher oil, so long-term borrowing costs ended that week lower.

v.h: Consumer sentiment revised up to 48.0, still a five-month low
v.s: The University of Michigan's final October sentiment index was 48.0, up from a preliminary 46.3 but below September's 48.1. Year-ahead inflation expectations were 4.7% and long-run expectations 3.5%, both up a tenth from September.
v.w: Weak sentiment with rising inflation expectations is the mix that keeps the Fed leaning toward a December hike while consumers pull back.

v.h: AI credit stress spreads: record junk spreads, CoreWeave and Oracle swaps near highs
v.s: Spreads on AI-related high-yield debt jumped 25 bp in a day to a record 360 bp over Treasuries while non-AI junk moved 2 bp. CoreWeave's 5-year CDS was about 1,066 bp on Oct 21 after a record near 1,195 bp on Oct 15; Oracle's was about 308 bp vs. 141 bp in January. AI-related debt issued in 2026 has passed $500B.
v.w: Stress at the biggest borrowers widens spreads for everyone, so loan quotes may not fall as much as Treasuries.

v.h: Blackstone: cap rates rose across its real estate in Q3; opportunistic funds fell 3.2%
v.s: Blackstone said valuation cap rates rose across its holdings in the third quarter on rate volatility. Opportunistic real estate funds fell 3.2% while core-plus gained 1.6%, and real estate distributable earnings fell 10% to $1.68B. Schwarzman said a higher cost of capital has hurt transaction activity.
v.w: The largest owner is marking values down on rates, which feeds the comps and appraisals lenders use for everyone else.

v.h: Lender schedules foreclosure auction for 30-unit Brighton apartment building
v.s: Selkirk Place Apartments, 56–58 Selkirk Place near Cleveland Circle, went to auction Oct 28. The owner financed its $12.8M 2022 purchase with an $8.75M loan; the city assesses the building at $7.24M, and a recent listing at $12.5M was cancelled.
v.w: A 2022 Boston apartment purchase now assessed below its loan shows how far values have reset for owners who bought at peak prices with floating or short-term debt.

v.h: 10-year Treasury falls below 5% in a flight to safety
v.s: The 10-year yield fell about 17 bp to 4.96%, its biggest one-day drop in more than two years and first close under 5% since late September, as investors moved into bonds during an AI-spending selloff that sent the Nasdaq down 2.6% (its worst day since June) and the S&P 500 down 1.2%. The 5-year fell 17 bp to 4.78%; the 2-year fell to 4.65% and the 30-year to 5.29%. Meta fell about 7% after raising the low end of its 2026 capex range to $135B.
v.w: A sub-5% 10-year eases refinance and cap-rate math, but a move driven by risk-off selling can reverse quickly.

v.h: Freddie Mac 30-year rate falls to 7.32%
v.s: Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed averaged 7.32%, down from 7.40%, ending a seven-week run without a decline; the 15-year fell to 6.68%. A year ago the 30-year was 6.19%. Mortgage News Daily's index fell 10 bp to 7.30% on Thursday.
v.w: Slightly lower mortgage rates help condo and small-multifamily exits, but buyers are still paying over a point more than a year ago.

v.h: Brent tops $112 after drone attack on Saudi oilfield
v.s: Brent settled at $112.92, up about 3.8%, after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone aimed at the Shaybah oilfield; debris killed two contractor workers. Reports that the U.S. and Israel are weighing new strikes on Iran added to the move, and WTI neared $100.
v.w: Higher oil feeds heating, diesel and construction input costs for New England owners heading into winter.

v.h: Jobless claims fall to 194,000, lowest since July
v.s: Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 from 200,000, the fewest in three months; the four-week average was 197,750. Weekly claims have not topped 230,000 this year.
v.w: Low layoffs support tenant demand and rent collections even as hiring stays slow.

v.h: 5-year TIPS auction clears at 2.367%, highest real yield in three years
v.s: Treasury sold $26B of new 5-year TIPS at a 2.367% real yield, slightly above the 2.36% when-issued level; bid-to-cover was 2.41, the lowest for a similar sale since April 2025. The implied 5-year inflation breakeven was about 2.41%.
v.w: High real yields, not inflation expectations, are what keep borrowing costs elevated for real estate.

v.h: Debt-sale delays top $5B, including Freddie Mac apartment-loan bonds
v.s: Companies postponed more than $5B of U.S. and European debt sales in October, the most this year. Freddie Mac pulled more than $440M of bonds backed by apartment mortgages and Mesirow shelved $175M of bonds tied to a Manhattan office tower. U.S. junk issuance fell to about $7B in October from $51B in September.
v.w: When agency apartment securitizations can't clear at target prices, multifamily loan spreads widen even as Treasuries rally.

v.h: 20-year bond reopening sells at 5.469% with a small tail
v.s: Treasury sold $13B of 20-year bonds at 5.469%, about 0.9 bp above the when-issued level. Bid-to-cover was 2.73 vs. a 2.62 average; directs took 31.6%, indirects 58.2% and dealers 10.3%.
v.w: Steady demand for long Treasuries helps cap long-term rates that drive permanent loan pricing.

v.h: Massachusetts constraints push more apartment investors to southern NH
v.s: Bisnow reports developers and investors are shifting to the I-93 corridor: Procopio is preparing a 310-unit build-to-rent project in Londonderry with a Rockland Trust construction loan, and Passco, TA Realty and Harbor Group have bought large Salem, Merrimack and Nashua communities. Colliers put NH apartment occupancy at 95.4% and average asking rent at $2,292, up 1.1%.
v.w: More capital and 4,000+ new units in southern NH mean more competition for acquisitions and softer rent growth in the region.

v.h: BGO buys leased Wrentham warehouse for $34.9M
v.s: BGO bought 545 Washington St. in Wrentham, a 132,055 SF Class A industrial building completed in 2023 and 100% leased to two tenants, from Bluewater Property Group and Affinius Capital. JLL represented the sellers.
v.w: About $264/SF for new, leased South Shore-area distribution is a fresh pricing marker for Route 1/I-495 industrial.

v.h: Liberty Mutual plans 85,000 SF Back Bay HQ expansion
v.s: Liberty Mutual filed a letter of intent to demolish three buildings on Stuart St. and Columbus Ave. and add a 23K SF vertical addition plus a 62K SF, 10-story building next to 157 Berkeley St. It plans to lease out its offices at 175 Berkeley St. and 30 St. James Ave. after consolidating.
v.w: Two large Back Bay office blocks coming to market would add sublease and direct supply to an already high-vacancy office market.

v.h: Poll: 65% back Question 7 to limit large minimum lot sizes
v.s: A UMass Amherst/WCVB poll found 65% of Massachusetts voters support the starter-homes ballot question, up from 59% in August, with 21% opposed and 10% undecided.
v.w: The vote turned out far closer than this poll suggested; smaller-lot zoning could open more suburban land if it passes.

v.h: Housing starts fall 5.2% in September to a 1.221M pace
v.s: Census said starts dropped to a 1.221M annual rate from a revised 1.288M in August, below the 1.310M consensus. Single-family starts fell 4.6% to 859,000, buildings with five or more units ran at 349,000, and permits slipped 0.2% to 1.400M.
v.w: Fewer starts with mortgages above 7% means less new supply competing with existing apartments in 2027–28.

v.h: 10-year eases to about 5.12% as oil reverses on Iran diplomacy hopes
v.s: Brent touched $111.99 after attacks on Gulf shipping, then settled at $108.79, down about 0.7%, on reports mediators were exploring a framework to revive U.S.-Iran talks; no breakthrough was confirmed. The 10-year fell about 2 bp to roughly 5.12%, helped by weak housing data, after rising to 5.15% on Monday.
v.w: Oil is still the swing factor for inflation and long rates, so cap-rate and refinancing math stays tied to Gulf headlines.

v.h: Somerville 120-unit portfolio sells for $39M
v.s: Three brick apartment buildings at 18 Day St., 49 Dover St. and 123 Orchard St. near Davis Square sold for $39M (about $325,000 per unit) after more than three rounds of bidding. Matthews represented the seller, which had held the buildings for more than a century; the buyer was not named.
v.w: Competitive bidding for older Red Line-adjacent apartments shows deep buyer demand for well-located Boston-area multifamily despite 5% Treasury yields.

v.h: Copper Mill sues partners over collapsed 754-unit Dorchester project
v.s: Copper Mill filed a nine-count suit in Suffolk Superior Court against site owners POB Capital and Pactolus Private Wealth Management over 75 Morrissey Blvd., a BPDA-approved two-tower, 754-unit plan. It alleges the owners moved to end their joint venture after the $67.5M purchase agreement while pursuing a deal valuing the site at $82.5M.
v.w: Another large approved Boston apartment project is stuck, which keeps new supply along Morrissey Blvd. further out.

v.h: Marcus & Millichap sees Boston office vacancy dipping to 19.1%
v.s: The firm expects metro vacancy to fall 10 bp year over year to 19.1% in Q4, the first annual decline since 2022, with asking rents up 1.2% to $38.75/SF. Cambridge vacancy rose 250 bp to 22.8%; average sale pricing fell from over $370/SF in 2022 to about $283/SF, with cap rates up from 6.7% to 7.7%.
v.w: Office pricing near $283/SF and 7.7% caps sets the bar for value-add and conversion bids.

v.h: Greystar opens 416-unit Juniper, last piece of its Everett build-out
v.s: Juniper at 201 Mill Road is Greystar's fifth and final community in Everett's Commercial Triangle, an $880M redevelopment totaling 1,905 apartments and 6,500 SF of retail. Construction began in summer 2024 and topped off in December 2025.
v.w: Another 416 units leasing up north of Boston adds near-term competition for Class A rents in Everett, Malden and Chelsea.

v.h: Troubled $22.4M office loan lifts Rockland Trust's bad loans 45%
v.s: Rockland Trust said nonperforming loans rose to $125.7M from $86.5M a year earlier, driven by a $22.4M office loan in workout whose tenant left; the building could become apartments. Delinquent loans rose to 0.73% of loans from 0.49%.
v.w: Local banks are still working through office problems, which keeps their CRE lending terms tight.

v.h: Nuveen: Treasuries rallied last week while credit spreads widened
v.s: Nuveen's weekly commentary said the 10-year fell 17 bp to 5.08% in the week to Oct 16, while the investment-grade spread widened to 84 bp, high yield to 331 bp and CMBS to 71 bp as some issuers postponed deals after hot inflation data.
v.w: Wider CMBS spreads offset part of the drop in Treasury yields, so all-in CRE loan coupons fell less than the 10-year.

v.h: Rising rates cloud Greater Boston apartment sales
v.s: Investment sales picked up after the rent control question was removed from the ballot in June, then slowed as rates rose; CBRE's Simon Butler said most buyers can absorb 25 to 30 bp of rate movement. Regional occupancy stayed above 95%, and Colliers counts 8,221 units under construction, down from more than 17,000 at the 2022 peak.
v.w: Rate swings widen bid-ask gaps on Boston multifamily, though the shrinking pipeline supports rents later.

TAKEAWAYS.label: Migration takeaways by generation
v: The biggest magnets have the softest rents

Dallas, Atlanta, Phoenix, Houston and Denver draw movers from all over, yet their rents are flat to falling and 55–67% of Zillow listings offer concessions: years of new supply are still being absorbed. Chicago and New York are the exception, with strong pull and rents up 4–5%. Low-pull Northeast and Rust Belt metros (Providence, Buffalo, Cleveland, Hartford) post solid gains on thin supply.
California and the Midwest lose the most

Counting out-of-state moves, California has the biggest net outflow, followed by Ohio, Oklahoma, Missouri and Michigan. Florida, Texas and Colorado gain the most. In New England, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island run negative while New Hampshire gains, mostly from Boston.
Boomers head for sun and smaller places

Phoenix is the single biggest Boomer magnet, pulling from the whole West and Upper Midwest. Florida is the top state by a wide margin, followed by the Carolinas and Arizona. Retirement-style metros like Lake Havasu, Fort Myers, Prescott and Charleston rank high.
Gen X spreads across the Sun Belt
Dallas and Atlanta lead, followed by Chicago, Nashville, Tampa and Houston. Moves skew regional: Gen Xers often go a few hours away rather than across the country.

Texas is the top state for Millennials and Dallas is by far the top metro, ahead of Atlanta and Houston. They also move to nearby, cheaper metros like Worcester from Boston and Lehigh Valley from New York.
Gen Z moves back into big cities

New York City and Chicago draw Gen Z from nearly every region, and Denver, LA and the Bay Area follow. Older New Yorkers and Chicagoans, meanwhile, mostly head for the suburbs, Florida and the Sun Belt.
